definition: A Siamese neural network (sometimes called a twin neural network) is an artificial neural network that uses the same weights while working in tandem on two different input vectors to compute comparable output vectors.
details: Often one of the output vectors is precomputed, thus forming a baseline against which the other output vector is compared. This is similar to comparing fingerprints but can be described more technically as a distance function for locality-sensitive hashing. It is possible to build an architecture that is functionally similar to a twin network but implements a slightly different function. This is typically used for comparing similar instances in different type sets. Uses of similarity measures where a twin network might be used are such things as recognizing handwritten checks, automatic detection of faces in camera images, and matching text queries with indexed documents. The perhaps most well-known application of twin networks are face recognition, where known images of people are precomputed and compared to an image from a turnstile or similar. It is not obvious at first, but there are two slightly different problems. One is recognizing a person among a large number of other persons, that is the facial recognition problem. explainer.lead: A Siamese neural network, sometimes called a twin neural network, uses the same weights on two different input vectors in tandem to compute comparable output vectors. It matters because one output can be precomputed as a baseline for comparison, enabling efficient similarity matching.

tiers.eli5: Two identical machines process two things at once so you can line up their results and see how alike they are, like comparing fingerprints.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers precompute one output vector as a baseline and compare new inputs against it, which is technically a distance function for locality-sensitive hashing. A pitfall is that architectures can look like twin networks but implement a slightly different function.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, the same weights operate in tandem on two different input vectors to produce comparable output vectors, compared via a distance function for locality-sensitive hashing; variants can be functionally similar but implement a slightly different function.

explainer.example: A stored image embedding is precomputed as a baseline, and a new image is passed through the same weighted network so the two vectors can be compared by distance.
